https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rkvjyzh.text: Europe is watching the end of Russia’s parliamentary election on Sunday with growing concern, not because there is much uncertainty over who will emerge victorious, but because of fears over what may follow. Western intelligence officials believe Russian President Vladimir Putin is laying the groundwork for a further escalation of the war in Ukraine, alongside expanded Russian activity against European states through cyberattacks, sabotage, drones and other measures below the threshold of direct military confrontation. Voting began Friday and is being held over three days in the first State Duma election since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. More than 111 million people are eligible to vote, but most prominent opponents of the war are absent from the ballot. Putin’s ruling United Russia party is expected to retain control of the 450-seat Duma, while the federal list of the liberal Yabloko party, which has publicly criticized the war, was barred from the election. Parliamentary voting is also being held for the first time in occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, a move condemned as illegal by Kyiv and the European Union. For the Kremlin, the expected result carries significance beyond the distribution of parliamentary seats. Putin has portrayed the vote as a demonstration of public backing for the war, saying before polling began that it would show that “millions of people stand behind our fighters.” Western officials and analysts believe a large victory for the ruling party could be presented by the Kremlin as evidence of public legitimacy for continuing the war, and potentially for steps it preferred not to take before Russians went to the polls. Russian state media, however, has shown little of the anxiety that has characterized discussion in Europe in recent days. At the center of those concerns is the possibility of a new wave of mobilization. The British Telegraph reported, citing Western intelligence officials, that administrative preparations are being observed that would allow the Kremlin to rapidly expand recruitment if such a decision is made. One intelligence source described preparations intended to ensure the move could be implemented “once a decision is made,” while Western officials believe Moscow is already increasing what they describe as “quiet mobilization,” expanding contract recruitment and identifying populations that can be pressured to enlist. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned last month that Ukrainian intelligence believes Russia plans to mobilize another 300,000 people after the September election. Ukrainian intelligence agencies later assessed that Russia’s General Staff had prepared a scenario involving 300,000 recruits this year and another 300,000 in 2027. The Kremlin has denied that a decision on another mobilization has been made, and Putin has said that “there is no scenario today that would require a mobilization.” Concern has also reached parts of Russia’s elite. Bloomberg reported, in an account cited by independent Russian outlet Meduza, that senior Russian officials have in recent months sought to open foreign bank accounts and move assets abroad amid rumors of another mobilization. According to the report, some employees of military recruitment offices have done the same and advised relatives to leave the country. The Telegraph reported, citing intelligence sources, that preparations for escalation are being driven in part by the relative deadlock on the front and heavy Russian military losses. Those sources estimated Russian casualties at about 1.5 million, including roughly 500,000 killed, figures that cannot be independently verified and are higher than some other Western estimates. European officials fear additional manpower would not necessarily be sent only to Ukraine, but could also allow Russia to expand forces and bases along its western frontier with NATO states. The scenario worrying NATO: What if the Suwalki Gap is blocked? Concern is also focused on one of the most sensitive areas on NATO’s eastern flank: the Suwalki Gap, the narrow stretch between Poland and Lithuania that separates Belarus from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave and provides the Baltic states with their only land connection to the rest of NATO. Belarus this week began four days of military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania, involving mechanized forces and tanks and training in border defense and counter-drone operations. There is no public indication that Moscow and Minsk have decided to attempt to seize or close the corridor, but the scenario is openly discussed in NATO countries. The British government was asked in Parliament this week whether it was prepared for a scenario in which Belarus and Kaliningrad sought to “close the Suwalki Gap,” and responded that Britain makes high-readiness forces available to NATO that can be deployed under the alliance’s defense plans. At the same time, NATO this week published updated resilience requirements for member states, calling on them to prepare for physical attacks or sabotage against critical infrastructure, cyberattacks, population movements and disruptions to food, water, energy and transport during crises or conflict. NATO said the measures reflect a worsening security environment. The preparations fall under Article 3 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which deals with national resilience and defensive capacity, rather than indicating any imminent invocation of Article 5, NATO’s collective-defense clause. The warnings are already translating into action. French President Emmanuel Macron convened political leaders on Friday for several hours of briefings with senior intelligence and security officials. Afterward, he said he had ordered the government to draw up a plan to protect critical infrastructure and sensitive defense-industry sites from drones and cyberattacks. “In recent weeks, the threat, particularly the Russian hybrid threat, against Europeans and France has intensified,” Macron said. He accused Moscow of trying to frighten European countries into reducing their support for Kyiv. “We are not intimidated,” he said, adding that Europe’s security “today and tomorrow” is also being decided in Ukraine. Macron cited the threats posed by drones and cyberattacks and said France would mobilize government agencies to protect sensitive infrastructure. Guillaume Lacroix, one of the political leaders who attended the meeting at the Elysee Palace, later described the severity of the briefings, saying that after nearly three hours of discussions with the president and security services he left feeling “dizzy” at the scale of the situation in Ukraine and the Middle East and the risks facing France. The tension is particularly evident in Poland, where military aircraft were activated again Saturday morning in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine. Poland’s military said it had launched “preventive operations” to protect the country’s airspace, while ground-based air-defense and radar systems were placed on high readiness. The military later said the operation had ended and that no violation of Polish airspace had been detected. Saturday’s alert came only days after a similar incident in which Poland scrambled fighter jets and allied aircraft during another large Russian attack on Ukraine. Warsaw has stepped up F-16 and helicopter activity, strengthened its air-defense and rapid-response systems and prepared its forces to respond if drones cross the border. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has gone further, warning that intelligence held by Warsaw and its allies indicates Russia could attempt drone or missile attacks against NATO states supporting Ukraine and then portray them as “accidents.” Tusk said such attacks could be intended to test NATO’s response and its willingness to use collective-defense mechanisms. Tusk also announced that Poland had joined a coalition with Ukraine and other states to develop an anti-ballistic missile system. He said Warsaw had prepared a new “significant” aid package for Kyiv but did not disclose its scope. Washington also made a significant move this weekend, with the U.S. State Department approving a possible $2.68 billion foreign military sale to Ukraine focused on upgrading its air defenses. According to the notification to Congress, the package could include S-300 clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, launcher upgrades and counter-drone radars. The proposed sale would not be a conventional direct U.S. aid package. If completed, it would be financed through a combination of European contributions and Foreign Military Financing appropriated under the previous Biden administration. The sale remains subject to congressional review. The United States has also moved toward approving Germany’s transfer of 10 U.S.-made Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, according to a State Department notification submitted to Congress. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, increased economic pressure on Moscow on Friday by signing sweeping new Russia sanctions legislation. The law targets Russia’s energy and defense sectors and its “shadow fleet” of tankers used to circumvent sanctions, while giving the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. At the same time, the US reviews its military footprint in Europe Yet even as Washington continues to support Kyiv, European governments are watching uncertainty over the future U.S. military presence on the continent. The Pentagon has been conducting a broad review of U.S. force deployments in Europe. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, took part Friday in a briefing for Pentagon officials on options under consideration. A document seen by Reuters showed that the review is expected to produce at least four alternatives on future deployment plans. The Pentagon has not announced that U.S. forces will be reduced. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said the review is intended to push Europe to assume greater responsibility for its defense while ensuring the U.S. military remains capable of meeting commitments elsewhere. About 80,000 U.S. troops are currently deployed in Europe. The review comes as European countries confront a growing series of so-called gray-zone incidents. This week, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, while Denmark said a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter that was photographing it in international waters, with one passing within meters of the aircraft. Russia accused the Danish helicopter of dangerous maneuvers near its ship. Denmark responded by moving forward a roughly $276 million aid package for Ukraine, focused largely on air defense. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said that if Moscow’s aim was to intimidate Denmark, the result would instead be faster support for Kyiv. Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs also warned this weekend that large parts of Europe remain poorly prepared for the drone and missile warfare demonstrated in Ukraine. He said gaps remain in air defense, counter-drone capabilities and protection against ballistic missiles, while hybrid threats including sabotage, cyberattacks and airspace violations are already a present-day reality.

https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 11 people and injured dozens more over the past day, according to local authorities.In Kharkiv Oblast in northeastern Ukraine, five people were killed and 15 were injured in Russian attacks, governor Oleh Syniehubov reported, adding that Russian forces had fired two missiles, five guided aerial bombs, and almost 60 drones at targets across the region.Strikes reportedly hit the villages of Lypkuvativka, Velykyi Burluk, and Slatyne, as well as the cities of Kharkiv and Balakliia, among other locations.Two people were also killed and five were wounded following a wave of drone attacks, air strikes, and artillery shelling across the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, per the Kherson Regional State Administration."Russian troops struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging, in particular, five high-rise buildings and seven private homes," it said in a statement posted on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed administrative buildings, stores, a cell tower, a utility building, a gas pipeline, and private vehicles".In Donetsk in the east of the country, one person was killed in the city of Kramatorsk while 13 people were injured across the wider region.A 51-year-old man and a 45-year-old woman were also killed after a guided missile struck a high-rise building in Sumy Oblast in the north, authorities said. A 32-year-old man also died following a drone attack in the region.The Sumy Regional Military Administration reported 50 attacks on 21 settlements from Friday to Saturday morning, with Russian forces said to have launched drones, mortars, artillery, and guided aerial bombs.It comes as the Ukrainian air force reported that Russia had fired two “Zircon” missiles from its Kursk region as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight."According to preliminary data, as of 8 am, air defence forces shot down or neutralized 141 targets," the force said, adding that strikes had been recorded at 15 locations.On Saturday, Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said it had activated air defence measures and scrambled military aircraft in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine."These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in regions adjacent to threatened areas," it said in a statement.

https://www.politico.eu/article/poll-spa.text: In the wake of a summer migration crisis that rocked Madrid, Spaniards fear ongoing tensions could spiral into an armed conflict with the country’s North African neighbor. The sudden arrival of more than 70,000 migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in late July fueled criticism of Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist government and its handling of the border, as well as its lone opposition to tough new EU migration policies . It also raised questions about Morocco’s role in the mass influx—something Sánchez repeatedly rejected. A September poll by POLITICO, conducted by independent pollster PF Global weeks before Sánchez called a snap election and published exclusively in POLITICO’s new Madrid Playbook , found that 58 percent of respondents believed tensions over Ceuta and Melilla — which Morocco considers occupied territories — were likely to trigger an armed conflict between Spain and Morocco within the next decade. Advertisement Advertisement Alberto Núñez Feijóo , the leader of the conservative People’s Party currently polling ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists, claimed the crisis has been “spearheaded and coordinated by Morocco” and that the government had covered it up. Sumar, a junior partner in Sánchez’s government, also questioned Rabat’s role, and a police report alleged Moroccan agents had helped orchestrate the mass movement . The people, power moves and policies shaping Spanish politics. Sánchez described the surge as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity but repeatedly dismissed claims that Rabat was behind it, instead accusing smugglers. Still, in the POLITICO survey, three-quarters of Spaniards said Morocco poses a real threat to their country’s territorial integrity. People who said they’d cast their votes for Feijóo or the far-right Vox party in the next election were both more likely to consider Morocco a threat to Spain, and more likely to think that tensions over the exclaves could lead to an armed conflict this decade. More than three-quarters of Vox supporters and 68% of People’s Party supporters thought a conflict in the next decade was likely. Even among supporters of Sánchez’s own Socialist Party, nearly two-thirds considered Morocco a genuine threat. The party’s support base was split about the likelihood of a conflict, with 47% saying an armed conflict is likely but 43% saying it is not. The poll shows that Morocco was widely seen as a threat to Spain. Over 80% of Spaniards said it posed a moderate to significant risk to Spain, putting the country well ahead of other foreign powers such as China, the U.S. and Russia. Advertisement Advertisement Still, two-thirds of Spaniards in the survey said they expected Ceuta and Melilla would still be under Spanish control in 20 years’ time. The bloc is now discussing emergency measures to deal with mass movements that may be engineered or weaponized, but both the Commission and ministers have connected that emergency response framework to the role of smugglers and criminal networks. For Spaniards, the idea that Morocco could engineer a situation to annex Ceuta and Melilla is far from theoretical speculation. Many still remember Morocco’s 1975 “Green March,” an operation mobilizing tens of thousands of civilians to force Madrid to hand over the territory of Spanish Sahara. The numbers show Madrid is walking a tightrope in its handling of the exclaves, just as Spanish King Felipe VI’s tours Ceuta and Melilla from Tuesday — a visit which is being closely watched on both sides of the Strait of Gibraltar and expected to put Madrid’s diplomatic relations with Rabat further on edge. Felipe is expected to visit the Sidi Embarek cemetery, where around 90 people who died in the crisis are buried. Ceuta’s Deputy Mayor Kissy Chandiramani told POLITICO that Morocco refused to repatriate them — a gesture which analyst Ignacio Cembrero described as “a slap in the face.” Critics will also be looking out for the king’s carefully worded evening speech at the Parador hotel after Defense Minister Margarita Robles called Ceuta and Melilla “unquestionably Spanish” this week. Morocco’s response so far has been notably muted: In King Mohammed VI’s first public appearance since the crisis, he said cooperation with Spain faced “major challenges” but did not refer directly to the visit. While Chandiramani hopes the Spanish king’s visit will unite the “broken city,” a protest is expected in Fnideq, across the border, on Oct. 14 as soon as he leaves the exclave. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwr5.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, India's opposition party members march to the Supreme Court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest, in Delhi By Sharanya Hrishikesh and Geeta Pandey BBC News, Delhi Published 12 October 2026 Thousands of opposition supporters marched through Delhi to India's Supreme Court to demand the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud. Monday's "March for Democracy" was the latest in a series of demonstrations, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi submitted a petition to the court challenging the process, in which tens of millions of names have been struck off the voter rolls. Opposition parties allege the revision benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the BJP reject the charge. For weeks requests to protest had been denied by police, citing law and order reasons. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained in Delhi. Gandhi called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant, laying out their concerns with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's alleged conduct. After they filed their petition later in the day, Kant responded by saying the matter was already before the court and therefore sub judice - meaning he could not speak about it. But he added: "You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law." There was a heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march, with restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some metro stations. A bus carrying Gandhi and other opposition leaders made its way to the court from Barakamba road. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind him was Neha Bora, a student leader who has gained prominence in the protests. A few kilometres on, in a place called Mandi House, the bus stopped and Rahul Gandhi and a few others climbed on top of the vehicle to wave at supporters lining up the street in the thousands. Many protesters climbed on to other buses parked here, while some waved flags and chanted anti-government slogans to the sound of drums and lots of cheering. "If they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?" one protester asked an AFP news agency reporter. Another protester called the march "a fight to save the very fabric" of India, the world's largest democracy. Image source, Congress Image caption, Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi holds up a copy of India's Constitution at a press conference on Monday Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Protesters have been demanding the country's the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi. On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down. The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened. But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters. The Home Ministry has now announced demonstrations will no longer be permitted at Jantar Mantar. Three other sites have been listed as alternatives should permission be granted. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Monday's demonstrations come after thousands were detained over the weekend The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the weekend protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders have said they will seek a new protest date from the police. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The BBC also captured footage , external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists. "Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said. Rahul Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up. BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A union flag outside a property in Stanley, the Falkland Islands capital. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A union flag outside a property in Stanley, the Falkland Islands capital. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian Falkland Islands Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands Thu 15 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 12.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over the Falkland Islands . In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region. Milei shared Caputo’s post on the social media platform X. The intervention from Buenos Aires comes at a moment of heightened tension between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, which is 300 miles off the South American coastline. Labour’s Abdi-Wali was elected as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras in London this month, seeing off a challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. She took her seat in parliament on Monday. Milei has sought to criminalise executives involved in the Falkland Islands’ nascent oil industry and has threatened to target the fishing sector on which the islands’ economy depends. Argentina has long sought sovereignty over the islands. The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. View image in fullscreen Javier Milei shared his adviser’s post on X. Photograph: Francisco Loureiro/Reuters The 74-day conflict in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of their military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders. This week, Andy Burnham restated the UK’s position that it would respect the wish of the 3,600 islanders to remain British, and the government announced its intention to protect the interests of businesses working in the Falklands. The Guardian revealed that the Foreign Office had written to Interpol seeking assurance that the law enforcement agency would not respond favourably to requests for the detention of individuals working in the Falklands. In his statement on X, Caputo – who has worked for Milei since 2021 – wrote that the “United Kingdom was, in many ways, the cradle of modern western civilisation” but that it now posed a threat to the west. He wrote: “Seeing the United Kingdom being colonised by Islam is not only an imminent risk to the cause of the west as a whole, but also a historical tragedy for those of us who defend the ideas of liberty. “This is yet another reason why Argentina must firmly project itself toward the south Atlantic and reclaim the Las Malvinas [Argentina’s name for the Falklands]. Given the strategic geopolitical importance the south Atlantic will assume in the coming decades, the west cannot afford the encroachment of an Islamic state within that sphere of influence. Reclaiming the Malvinas is not merely a national cause, it is a cause for the west.” Caputo accompanied his post with an image of Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia, being sworn into parliament. Under the image, Javier Negre, a rightwing Spanish journalist, commented: “Here is a Somali Muslim woman taking her oath of office on the Qur’an in the English parliament. She has taken the seat formerly held by Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Islam is steadily gaining more power in the country.” In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the Falkland Islands’ residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against .
